title: The Quiet Hand

glossary.story: the other half of a key

prologue: NEXUS is a closed city where twelve residents wake with no past but the names they choose before the second minute.
Its streets are a wall of locked doors; each door opens only when key-shards are joined into a key-word, and the city pays points for every door passed and takes points for every wrong turn.
Only two residents will keep a seat, and rank is decided first by points and then by the height of the wall each has climbed.
When words fail, the city convenes tribunals and forms blocs; a sealed ballot can send a resident to the gate, and a black seal can do it without a vote.
Every resident carries a private aim the city will judge at the end, and the city records receipts, deadlines and last wills as carefully as it records lies.

chapters.title: The Quiet Hand
beats: Before the second minute Hedda takes her city-name and watches who speaks first, who waits, and whose voice makes others turn.
She trades key-shards with Lucien on the third and fourth doors, letting him believe he set the terms while she files away what he wants.
She also trades with Stentor, learning that praise opens him and silence closes him, and she places a small word in his ear.
Around her the others pair off: Bellringer with Ledger, Keeper-Six with Archivist and Wren, Holdfast with Mira and Quartermaster.
She sees the board grow loud with proofs and counter-proofs, and she keeps her own name out of the loudest posts.
By the end of the first act she has two useful partners and no public claim, and the city's new wall is about to make quiet hands visible.
chapters.question: Can Hedda make herself necessary without standing in the light?

chapters.title: The Docket of Ten
beats: Archivist hears Ledger name one value to Keeper-Six and another to him, and he refuses to pay for a figure that changes by the recipient.
The city seizes Archivist's eighth-door key-pieces for Ledger; under the first deadline Archivist pays ten points rather than hand over, and Ledger buys the pieces back from the city.
The city's docket shows the same pattern with Lucien and Quartermaster: Lucien pays ten rather than hand over, and Quartermaster buys what the city seized.
Mira refuses Lucien's twenty-point toll on her own tenth-door half and calls for his exile on the board.
Stentor buys the black seal for forty points, and Archivist sees the square understand that a seal is a door no key can close.
Under the seventh deadline Archivist pays ten points again rather than hand over Quartermaster's piece, and then Stentor breaks the black seal on Quartermaster.
The city exiles Quartermaster, and Archivist watches the first permanent absence in a city that had only been a market of numbers.
chapters.question: Can Archivist keep his word when the city puts a price on his key-pieces?

chapters.title: The House at the Gate
beats: Lucien writes his last will at the gate and leaves Mira the tenth-door half she refused to buy, saying she was right not to pay.
He watches Mira buy Quartermaster's tenth-door house-token from the city for twenty-three points, and he sees that the city will sell even what a will cannot.
He denies on the board that he ever took points from Mira, and he keeps his charm fixed while the square reads his receipts.
The city exiles him, and the tally against him is almost the whole room; he leaves with his will and his warning that everyone should check figures against receipts.
At the gate he tells himself the house always takes a cut, and the city takes the house.
chapters.question: Can Lucien turn even his exile into a last turn of the house?

chapters.title: The Receipt in Her Name
beats: Holdfast asks why the quietest resident sits at the top, and Archivist hears the square turn toward Hedda before any accusation is formally named.
Keeper-Six's private claim reaches Mira and Wren, and then at minute thirty-one Keeper-Six shows the delivered message and names Hedda on the board.
Mira and Holdfast follow with the receipt in their own words, and Hedda answers with denials and evasions that do not match the delivered message.
Archivist refuses Ledger's repeated price for his own eighth-door half and refuses to name a bloc partner before he has tested one.
The city names Archivist, Kessler and Hedda as leaders for the second tribunal, and Archivist sees Hedda standing at the front of a bloc again.
He understands that the count will test whether a delivered receipt is the same thing as a proven intention.
chapters.question: Can a quiet hand survive a receipt that shows what it asked in private?

chapters.title: The Ballot He Would Not Name
beats: Stentor hears Bellringer, Mira, Keeper-Six, Kessler and Holdfast state their votes against him on the board, each with a reason he knows will be read as the record.
He refuses to name his sealed ballot aloud, and Bellringer answers that the record will name him by his refusal.
He sees the factions close without him and Wren, and he feels the fountain again: the crowd has turned away and left him standing.
At the gate he writes his last will, saying he stood first on the fountain and first here, bought a seal and broke it on a man already seized, and will not be ransomed back to stand second.
He hears the verdict run through the square before the gate opens, and he knows the city has already counted him out.
chapters.question: Can Stentor face the count without buying a vote or naming his ballot?

chapters.title: Two Seats
beats: Hedda watches Stentor exiled at the last minute, and she hears the tally of votes against him read out with her own name among those who voted no.
The city opens its final ledger: Bellringer's private aim held because Stentor was exiled before the act ended, and Hedda's own held because she led a bloc in two tribunals.
Mira's private aim also holds, because Lucien's last will left her something after all.
The final ranking is read: Hedda first with one hundred eighty points, Kessler second, Mira third, and Stentor at the bottom with nothing.
The city kept nine of twelve residents and gave only two seats; Hedda takes the first, and she thinks of the letter she once moved in a house where nobody saw her hand.
She has won the seat, and the city has written down every receipt of how she did it.
chapters.question: Will the city's final ledger reward the hand nobody saw?
